\[
b(q) = \left\lfloor \frac{L\, Y(q)}{256} \right\rfloor,
\quad
b^* = \arg\max_b \#\{q \in W(p) : b(q) = b\},
\quad
C'(p) = \operatorname{mean}\{C(q) : q \in W(p),\ b(q) = b^*\},
\qquad L = 20,\ r = 3
\]

The formula shows the default parameter values.

where

- \(Y\): The luma of a pixel
- \(b(q)\): The bin of pixel q
- \(W(p)\): The window around pixel p
- \(L\): The number of bins

Y is the luma 0.2126 R + 0.7152 G + 0.0722 B and W(p) the square window of side 2r + 1 around the pixel. The luma values fall into L equal bins. The most common bin in the window wins, and ties go to the darker bin. The output is the mean color of the window pixels in that bin. So a pixel takes the color of the brightness that most of its neighbors share, and small details vanish into patches. OpenCV's xphoto module implements this effect and cites Holzmann's book for it. OpenCV leaves pixels outside the image out of the window and quantizes the result. Here the window follows the border mode, and nothing is quantized.
